extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners assessing subject-matter eligibility for nature-based product claims
extracted.subtask_description: A step-by-step worksheet to guide examiners through 35 U.S.C. 101 subject-matter eligibility analysis for claims involving nature-based products, following the 2014 Interim Eligibility Guidance and July 2015 Update. Covers claim construction (BRI), Step 1 statutory category, Step 2A identification of judicial exceptions (product of nature, law of nature, natural phenomenon, abstract idea) including the 'markedly different characteristics' test, and Step 2B assessing whether additional elements provide 'significantly more' (an inventive concept).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify what applicant invented
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the disclosure to identify what applicant considers as the invention (MPEP 2103(I)). This can be a brief description and should not merely reproduce the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The take away should focus on the invention (e.g., 'a mixture of texiol and water'). Use this identification to inform the subsequent SME analysis and inventive-concept evaluation; it helps relate additional elements to what applicant actually invented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Construe the claim in accordance with its broadest reasonable interpretation based on the specification’s definitions and plain meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: BRI of a dietary sweetener claim = a mixture of texiol and water in specified amounts (1-5% texiol and at least 90% water). Note that BRI may exclude naturally occurring counterparts if amounts/limitations differ (e.g., sap contains ~10% texiol and thus is not encompassed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — statutory category determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claimed invention falls within one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If yes, continue SME analysis. If no, make a rejection that the claim is drawn to non-statutory subject matter (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01). If the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, it is recommended to continue the analysis under that assumption and make the assumption clear in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A — identify whether claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a product of nature, a law of nature, a natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim is 'directed' to a product of nature when it recites a nature-based product limitation that does not exhibit markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart. For other exceptions, it is sufficient to identify that the claimed concept aligns with a judicial exception (no bright lines between types). Use case law charts and the 2014 Guidance for assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to nature-based product limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim recites nature-based product limitations, apply the 'markedly different characteristics' test to those limitations to determine if they are product-of-nature exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-limiting examples of characteristics considered: biological or pharmacological functions/activities; chemical and physical properties; phenotype including functional and structural characteristics; and structure/form (chemical, genetic, physical). The analysis should be applied only to the nature-based product limitations within the claim (not necessarily to the whole claim if other non-nature elements are present).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process-claim exception for markedly different analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that a process claim generally is not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products used in the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited exception: if a process claim is drafted such that there is no difference in substance from a product claim (e.g., 'a method of providing an apple'), then the analysis may be applicable. Otherwise evaluate process claims under the appropriate exception analysis (e.g., law of nature/natural phenomenon/abstract idea).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify nature-based limitation(s) and closest naturally occurring counterpart
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Identify the limitation(s) in the claim that set forth or describe a nature-based product; (b) identify the closest naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state for comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (a) 'the claimed mixture of texiol and water'; (b) 'the naturally occurring texiol-water mixture in the sap of the Texas mint plant.' Judicial exceptions need not be old or long-prevalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare claimed limitation to counterpart for 'markedly different characteristics'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the claimed nature-based product limitation to its naturally occurring counterpart to determine whether it exhibits markedly different characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed product exhibits markedly different characteristics, it is not a product-of-nature exception. If it lacks markedly different characteristics (e.g., components retain the same structure, function, and properties), then the limitation is a product-of-nature exception and you must proceed to Step 2B. Record the reasoning (choose (i) or (ii) and explain). Examples: retention of sweetness/bitter aftertaste indicates no marked difference; altered organoleptic property (neutralization of bitter aftertaste by Compound N) may indicate a marked difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: If directed to other exceptions, identify exception limitations and explain why
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon, identify the limitation(s) that recite the exception and explain why the recited subject matter is an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the limitation(s) and articulate the reasons (e.g., it recites a mathematical relationship, fundamental economic practice, natural principle, etc.). Use court-case discussions and the abstract-idea chart in the July 2015 Update for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — identify additional elements beyond the exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether there are any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the identified judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim is a product of nature comprising a combination of components that do not occur together in nature as claimed, treat each component as an additional element to the others for purposes of this inquiry. If there are no additional elements, conclude the SME analysis with a §101 rejection (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015) and consider whether disclosure contains elements that could be suggested to applicant to render a claim eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate significance of additional elements — search for an 'inventive concept'
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider identified additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether the claim as a whole amounts to 'significantly more' than the exception(s) (i.e., contains an inventive concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons supporting significance can include one or more of the following: improves another technology or technical field; improves the functioning of a computer itself; applies the exception with, or by use of, a particular machine (not a generic computer performing generic functions); effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing; adds a specific limitation other than what is well-understood, routine and conventional in the field (not appending routine activities at high generality); adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application (not insignificant extra-solution activity like mere data gathering); adds meaningful limitations amounting to more than generally linking use of the exception to a particular technological environment. Also note: not adding the words 'apply it' or equivalent phraseology and not merely using a generic computer are negative factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide eligibility based on inventive-concept evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: If any additional elements, individually or in combination, amount to significantly more than the exception(s), conclude the claim is eligible; if not, conclude the claim is ineligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If eligible, continue examination under other patentability requirements and optionally clarify reasoning in Office action. If ineligible, make a §101 rejection (use Form Paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015) and identify any elements in the disclosure that could be added to claims to attempt to achieve eligibility (e.g., adding 1-2% of Compound N to the sweetener). Examples and case law (e.g., Funk Brothers, Myriad, Roslin) are provided to illustrate outcomes and reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis option
rubrics_metrics.description: When eligibility is self-evident and the claim clearly does not attempt to tie up an exception such that others cannot practice it, use a streamlined analysis and conclude SME analysis without a full write-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to February 2015 Training Slides for examples of when streamlined analysis is appropriate. If using assumptions (e.g., assuming an amendment yields a statutory category), make those assumptions clear in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action / record-keeping guidance and sample rejection language
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on documenting SME conclusions in Office actions, including sample rejection language and form-paragraph references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample rejection language provided (e.g., 'Claim X is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception ... without significantly more'). Use Form Paragraphs 7.05, 7.05.01, 7.05.015 as appropriate. Clarify reasoning in the record where helpful (e.g., explain why claim is directed to a nature-based product or why additional elements do/don't provide significantly more).
